name: Electricity as GPT

lesson.title: Why Factories Took Forty Years to Notice They Didn't Need a Central Engine
lesson.summary: Electricity passes every test of a general purpose technology, but its most famous lesson is the decades-long lag between having the technology and actually redesigning industry around it.
lesson.body:
Applying the same three test General Purpose Technology framework to electricity turns up a history with an unusually well documented and genuinely counterintuitive lag between technical availability and real economic impact.

Central power generation and distribution became commercially practical in the 1880s, associated first with Thomas Edison's direct current systems and soon after with the alternating current systems championed by George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla, whose greater efficiency over long transmission distances eventually won out. Once distribution existed, electricity's applicability turned out to be about as broad as a GPT can get: lighting first, then motors for essentially every kind of machinery, then telecommunications, refrigeration, and eventually the entire electronics industry that later chapters of this book depend on.

Test two, improvement over time, played out much as it did for the steam engine: generation efficiency, transmission losses, and motor design all improved substantially across the following decades, and each improvement made new categories of use economically viable that simply were not viable at earlier price points and reliability levels.

The genuinely instructive part of this history for a skeptic's toolkit is what economic historians, notably Paul David in influential research from around 1990, called the productivity paradox of electrification. Factories that switched from steam to electric power in the early years mostly just replaced their single large central steam engine with a single large central electric motor, keeping the same line shaft and belt factory layout that had been designed around one central power source all along. Measured productivity gains from this first wave of electrification were modest, disappointingly so relative to the technology's promise. The real gains arrived only once factory owners redesigned their factories around unit drive, a small electric motor on every individual machine, which allowed flexible layouts, individual machine control, and floor plans organized around workflow rather than around proximity to a central engine. That redesign took decades, roughly a generation, to become standard practice.

Test three, enabling new innovation: electrification did not just power existing machines more conveniently. It made the modern assembly line and factory logistics practical, enabled entirely new industries built around electric appliances and later electronics, and became the physical substrate that the transistor and the internet, both covered in the next two chapters, were ultimately built on top of.

The lesson worth carrying forward is specific: even a technology that unambiguously passes all three GPT tests can show weak or disappointing productivity numbers for a long stretch, not because the technology has failed but because the complementary organizational and infrastructural changes needed to use it well lag behind its raw availability. A skeptic evaluating any new technology's underwhelming early productivity numbers should ask whether the shortfall reflects a fundamental limit, or simply this same adjustment lag playing out again.
